question.text:
Given that the random variable $X\sim B(100,0.4),$ use the normal approximation to the binomial distribution to approximate $P(X=50).$ Give your final answer to three decimal places

Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $\Phi(z)$ for the standard normal distribution.

$z$$\, 0.04 \,$$\, 0.05 \,$$\, 0.06 \,$
$\, 1.9 \,$ $\, 0.9738 \,$ $\, 0.9744 \,$ $\, 0.9750 \,$
$\, 2.0 \,$ $\, 0.9793 \,$ $\, 0.9798 \,$ $\, 0.9803 \,$
$\, 2.1 \,$ $\, 0.9838 \,$ $\, 0.9842 \,$ $\, 0.9846 \,$
$\, 2.2 \,$ $\, 0.9875 \,$ $\, 0.9878 \,$ $\, 0.9881 \,$
$\, 2.3 \,$ $\, 0.9904 \,$ $\, 0.9906 \,$ $\, 0.9909 \,$
question.explanation:
Given a binomial random variable $X \sim B(n,p),$ if

  • $np > 5,$ and

  • $n(1-p) > 5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p),$ that is,

\[ Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)). \]

Here, we have $n=100$ and $p = 0.4.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 100\cdot 0.4\\[5pt] &= 40 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 100\cdot (1-0.4) \\[5pt] &=60 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

\[ \mu = np = (100)(0.4) = 40 \]

and variance

\[ \sigma^2 = np(1-p) = (100)(0.4)(1-0.4) = 24. \]

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y \sim N(40, 24).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X = 50).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

\[ P(X = 50) \approx P(49.5 \leq Y \leq 50.5). \]

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

\[ \begin{align*} P(49.5 \leq Y \leq 50.5) &= P \left( \dfrac{49.5-40}{\sqrt{24}} \leq Z \leq \dfrac{50.5-40}{\sqrt{24}} \right) \\[5pt] &\approx P \left( 1.94 \leq Z \leq 2.14 \right) \\[5pt] &= P(Z \leq 2.14) - P(Z < 1.94) \\[5pt] &= P(Z \leq 2.14) - P(Z \leq 1.94) \\[5pt] &= \Phi(2.14) - \Phi(1.94) \\[5pt] &=0.9838 - 0.9738\\[5pt] &=0.010 \end{align*} \]

Therefore,

\[ P(X = 50)\approx 0.010. \]

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0102.$

example.title: Using a Normal Approximation to Approximate a Binomial Probability

question.text:
Which of the following probabilities could be approximated using the normal approximation of the binomial distribution?

  1. The probability that a student correctly solves $4$ questions in a $5$-question math test if the student has a $75\%$ probability of correctly answering each question.
  2. The probability that $42$ flights out of $120$ arrive early at an airport if the probability of a single flight arriving early is $0.45$ for each flight.
  3. The probability of getting $4$ ones on $10$ rolls of a $4$-sided die.
question.explanation:
Given a binomial random variable $X \sim B(n,p),$ if

  • $np > 5,$ and

  • $n(1-p) > 5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p),$ that is,

\[ Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)). \]

Let's now examine each situation.

  • In situation I, we have $n=5$ and $p=0.75.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 5\cdot 0.75\\[5pt] &= 3.75\\[5pt] &\ngtr 5.\quad {\color{red}{\times}}\\[5pt] \end{align*} So, we cannot use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

  • In situation II, we have $n=120$ and $p=0.45.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 120\cdot 0.45\\[5pt] &= 54 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 120\cdot (1-0.45) \\[5pt] &=66 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

  • In situation III, we have $n=10$ and $p=\dfrac14.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 10\cdot \dfrac14\\[5pt] &= 2.5\\[5pt] &\ngtr 5.\quad {\color{red}{\times}}\\[5pt] \end{align*} So, we cannot use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

example.title: Identifying Situations Where a Normal Approximation is Appropriate

question.text:
An archer practices firing an arrow at a target $60$ times. The archer has a $44\%$ chance of hitting the bull's eye. Using the normal approximation to the binomial distribution, estimate the probability that the archer hits the bull's eye more than $30$ times. Give your final answer to three decimal places.

Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $\Phi(z)$ for the standard normal distribution.

$z$$\, 0.05 \,$$\, 0.06 \,$$\, 0.07 \,$
$\, 0.9 \,$ $\, 0.8289 \,$ $\, 0.8315 \,$ $\, 0.8340 \,$
$\, 1.0 \,$ $\, 0.8531 \,$ $\, 0.8554 \,$ $\, 0.8577 \,$
$\, 1.1 \,$ $\, 0.8749 \,$ $\, 0.8770 \,$ $\, 0.8790 \,$
question.explanation:
Given a binomial random variable $X \sim B(n,p),$ if

  • $np > 5,$ and

  • $n(1-p) > 5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p),$ that is,

\[ Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)). \]

Here, we have $n=60$ and $p = 0.44.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 60\cdot 0.44\\[5pt] &= 26.4 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 60\cdot (1-0.44) \\[5pt] &=33.6 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

\[ \mu = np = (60)(0.44) = 26.4 \]

and variance

\[ \sigma^2 = np(1-p) = (60)(0.44)(1-0.44) = 14.784. \]

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y \sim N(26.4, 14.784).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(X > 30).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

\[ P(X > 30) = P(X \geq 31) \approx P(Y \geq 30.5). \]

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

\[ \begin{align*} P(Y \geq 30.5) &= P \left( Z \geq \dfrac{30.5 - 26.4}{ \sqrt{14.784} } \right) \\[5pt] &\approx P(Z \geq 1.07) \\[5pt] &= 1-P(Z< 1.07) \\[5pt] &= 1 - P(Z\leq1.07) \\[5pt] &= 1 - \Phi( 1.07) \\[5pt] &=1-0.8577 \\[5pt] &=0.1423 \end{align*} \]

Therefore,

\[ P(X > 30) \approx 0.142. \] Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.1431.$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p),$ that is,

\[ Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)). \]

Here, we have $n=70$ and $p = 0.5.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 70\cdot 0.5\\[5pt] &=35 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 70\cdot (1-0.5) \\[5pt] &=35 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

\[ \mu = np = (70)(0.5) = 35 \]

and variance

\[ \sigma^2 = np(1-p) = (70)(0.5)(1-0.5) = 17.5. \]

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y \sim N(35, 17.5).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X = 30).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

\[ P(X = 30) \approx P(29.5 \leq Y \leq 30.5). \]

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

\[ \begin{align*} P(29.5 \leq Y \leq 30.5) &= P \left( \dfrac{29.5-35}{\sqrt{17.5}} \leq Z \leq \dfrac{30.5-35}{\sqrt{17.5}} \right) \\[5pt] &\approx P \left( -1.31 \leq Z \leq -1.08 \right) \\[5pt] &= P(Z \leq -1.08) - P(Z < -1.31) \\[5pt] &= P(Z \leq -1.08) - P(Z \leq -1.31) \\[5pt] &= \Phi(-1.08) - \Phi(-1.31) \\[5pt] &= 0.1401 - 0.0951 \\[5pt] &= 0.045 \end{align*} \]

\[ P(X = 30)\approx 0.045. \]

Given a binomial random variable $X \sim B(n,p),$ if

  • $np > 5,$ and

  • $n(1-p) > 5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p),$ that is,

\[ Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)). \]

Here, we have $n=100$ and $p = 0.5.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 100\cdot 0.5\\[5pt] &= 50 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 100\cdot (1-0.5) \\[5pt] &=50 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

\[ \mu = np = (100)(0.5) = 50 \]

and variance

\[ \sigma^2 = np(1-p) = (100)(0.5)(1-0.5) = 25. \]

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y \sim N(50, 25).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(43 < X \lt 53).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

\[ P(43 < X \lt 53) = P(44 \leq X \leq 52) \approx P(43.5 \leq Y \leq 52.5). \]

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

\[ \begin{align*} P(43.5 \leq Y \leq 52.5) &= P\left(\dfrac{43.5-50}{\sqrt{25}} \leq Z \leq \dfrac{52.5-50}{\sqrt{25}}\right) \\[5pt] &\approx P \left( -1.30 \leq Z \leq 0.50 \right) \\[5pt] &= P(Z\leq 0.50) - P(Z < -1.30) \\[5pt] &= P(Z\leq 0.50) - P(Z \leq -1.30) \\[5pt] &=\Phi(0.50)-\Phi(-1.30) \\[5pt] &=0.6915 - 0.0968 \\[5pt] &=0.5947 \end{align*} \]

Therefore,

\[ P(43 \lt X \lt 53) \approx 0.595. \] Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.5947.$
